q: Which painter, while painting a screen for Sun Quan, let a drop of ink fall on the silk by mistake and turned it into a fly — so lifelike that Sun Quan took it for a real fly and raised his hand to flick it away?
reply:
The painter was **Cao Buxing** (曹不興).

The account appears in Pei Songzhi's annotation quoting the *Wu Lu* (《吳錄》), attached to the biography of Zhao Da in the *Book of Wu*, in a passage listing men and women of Wu famed for special skills:

「曹不興善畫，權使畫屏风，誤落筆點素，因就以作蠅。既進御，權以爲生蠅，舉手彈之。」[1]

That is: "Cao Buxing was skilled at painting. Quan had him paint a screen; by mistake his brush dropped and made a dot on the white silk, so he went on to make it into a fly. When it was presented to the throne, Quan took it for a live fly and raised his hand to flick it away." [1]

This matches your question in every particular: the ink blot on the silk, the fly painted from it, and Sun Quan mistaking it for a live fly and swatting at it. Note that it is Pei Songzhi quoting the *Wu Lu* rather than Chen Shou's own narrative [1]. The same passage names the eight people contemporaries called the "Eight Excellences" (八絕) — Cao Buxing together with the calligrapher Huang Xiang, the Go player Yan Wu, the dream-interpreter Song Shou, the physiognomist Zheng Yu of Gu City, and Wu Fan, Liu Dun and Zhao Da:

「孤城鄭嫗能相人，及範、惇、達八人，世皆稱妙，謂之八絕云。」[1]

q: A wealthy man gave a ride to a woman on the road. She told him she was a messenger from Heaven sent to burn down his house, but because he had been kind to her she let him go home first and move his valuables out. Who was this wealthy man?
reply:
The wealthy man was **Mi Zhu** (麋竺, style Zizhong), a native of Quxian in Donghai Commandery.

His biography in the 《三国志》 establishes both his identity and his wealth: 「麋竺字子仲，東海朐人也。祖世貨殖，僮客萬人，貲產鉅億。」[18] The same biography notes his younger brother Mi Fang (「竺弟芳為彭城相」[18]) and his later attachment to Liu Bei (「謙卒，竺奉謙遺命，迎先主于小沛」[18]).

The story you describe is preserved in Pei Songzhi's commentary, which quotes the 《搜神記》: 「竺嘗從洛歸，未達家數十里，路傍見一婦人，從竺求寄載。行可數里，婦謝去，謂竺曰：「我天使也，當往燒東海麋竺家，感君見載，故以相語。」竺因私請之，婦曰：「不可得不燒。如此，君可馳去，我當緩行，日中火當發。」竺乃還家，遽出財物，日中而火大發。」[1]

In English: Mi Zhu was once returning from Luoyang; still some tens of *li* short of home, he saw a woman by the roadside who asked him for a ride. After about a few *li* she thanked him and took her leave, saying to him: "I am a messenger of Heaven; I am to go and burn the house of Mi Zhu of Donghai. Moved by your giving me a ride, I tell you this." Mi Zhu privately pleaded with her. She said: "It cannot be avoided; it must burn. In that case, you may gallop home; I will walk slowly, and the fire will start at noon." Mi Zhu then went home, hurriedly carried out his valuables, and at noon the fire indeed broke out.

由此看, the detail that he had valuables to carry out in haste fits the biography's account of his vast estate [18]. But the tale itself is cited from the 《搜神記》 in Pei's commentary [1], not found in Mi Zhu's own biography [18]; it should therefore be treated as a marvel recorded there, not as an attested historical event.

q: A woman from Jiuquan avenged her father by stabbing his killer to death in broad daylight in front of the city post-house, then went to the county office and gave herself up. Who was she, and in which year did this happen?
reply:
She was Pang E — Chen Shou's main text calls her "the mother of Yu, E" (淯母娥), while Pei Songzhi's note quoting Huangfu Mi's *Lie Nü Zhuan* calls her "Pang E-qin" (龐娥親). She was from Luofu in Jiuquan, wife of Pang Zixia and daughter of Zhao Jun'an (the main text writes "Zhao An"), and mother of Pang Yu. It happened in the first ten days of the second month of Guanghe 2, i.e. AD 179.

The main text of the *Wei Shu* biography of Pang Yu says: 「初，淯外祖父趙安為同縣李壽所殺，淯舅兄弟三人同時病死，壽家喜。淯母娥自傷父讎不報，乃幃車袖劍，白日刺壽於都亭前，訖，徐詣縣，顏色不變，曰：『父讎己報，請受戮。』祿福長尹嘉解印綬縱娥，娥不肯去，遂強載還家。會赦得免，州郡嘆貴，刊石表閭。」[3] — "At first, Yu's maternal grandfather Zhao An was killed by Li Shou of the same county; Yu's uncles, three brothers, all died of illness at the same time, and Li Shou's household rejoiced. Yu's mother E, grieving that her father's vendetta was unavenged, screened her carriage and hid a sword in her sleeve, and in broad daylight stabbed Li Shou in front of the post-house; this done, she walked calmly to the county office, her expression unchanged, and said: 'My father's vendetta is now avenged; I ask to receive execution.' The chief of Luofu, Yin Jia, took off his seal and cord and let E go; E refused to leave, so she was forcibly carried home. She happened to meet with a pardon and escaped punishment; the province and commandery admired and honored her, and had a stone inscribed to commend her village gate."

The year appears only in Pei's note quoting the *Lie Nü Zhuan*: she 「遂棄家事，乘鹿車伺壽。至光和二年二月上旬，以白日清時，於都亭之前，與壽相遇」[12] — "So she abandoned her household duties and rode a small cart to lie in wait for Li Shou. In the first ten days of the second month of Guanghe 2, at a clear hour of the day, she met Shou in front of the post-house" — and after the struggle 「遂拔其刀以截壽頭，持詣都亭，歸罪有司，徐步詣獄，辭顏不變」[12] — "she drew his own sword and cut off Shou's head, carried it to the post-house, gave herself up to the authorities, and walked slowly to the prison, her speech and countenance unchanged." Guanghe 2 is AD 179.

Pei's note also supplies background the main text omits: she was 「表氏龐子夏之妻，祿福趙君安之女也」, and her three younger brothers had all 「皆欲報仇」 but died in a plague, whereupon Li Shou rejoiced, saying 「趙氏強壯已盡，唯有女弱，何足復憂」, and his guard slackened [2]. Afterward the Inspector of Liang Province, Zhou Hong, the Grand Administrator of Jiuquan, Liu Ban, and others 「並共表上，稱其烈義，刊石立碑，顯其門閭」; Zhang Huan 「以束帛二十端禮之」; and the late Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Liang Kuan wrote her biography [1].

One point to note: Chen Shou's main text gives no year; the date "Guanghe 2" appears only in Pei's note quoting the *Lie Nü Zhuan*.

q: P'ei Sung-chih's commentary records a Wei Grand Administrator of a frontier commandery: Sun Ch'üan suddenly arrived with tens of thousands of men, rain had washed out the city palisade and there was no time to repair it, so he ordered everyone in the city to hide while he himself lay in his quarters and did not get up, and Sun Ch'üan withdrew, suspecting an ambush. Who was this man? What difference does P'ei Sung-chih note between this account and the man's main biography?
reply:
This man was **Wen Ping 文聘**, Grand Administrator (太守) of Jiangxia (江夏) in Wei. The story comes from Pei Songzhi's commentary citing the *Weilüe* 魏略, attached to Wen Ping's biography in the *Weishu*.

**The account (Pei's note, citing *Weilüe*):**

q: In the first year of Huangwu, the Wu fleet ran into a great storm at Dongkou and many ships capsized. Men in the water clung to the big ships and cried for help, but the other ships pushed them off with halberds and spears. Who ordered that those in the water be hauled aboard, and how many were saved?
reply:
**Wu Can (吾粲) and Huang Yuan (黃淵) gave the order, and together they saved over a hundred men.**

The account is in Wu Can's biography in the *Book of Wu*. In the first year of Huangwu (222 CE, per the era conversion), Wu Can was serving with Lü Fan (呂範), He Qi (賀齊) and others, commanding the naval force that faced the Wei general Cao Xiu (曹休) at Dongkou. A great storm struck:

「黃武元年，與呂范、賀齊等俱以舟師拒魏將曹休於洞口。值天大風，諸船綆紲斷絕，漂沒著岸，為魏軍所獲，或覆沒沉溺，其大船尚存者，水中生人皆攀緣號呼，他吏士恐船傾沒，皆以戈矛撞擊不受。」[1]

That is: the cables of the ships snapped, some drifted ashore and were captured by the Wei army, others capsized and drowned; the survivors in the water clung to the hulls of the larger ships that were still afloat and cried out, while the other officers and men, fearing their own ships would be swamped, beat them off with halberds and spears.

It was Wu Can and Huang Yuan who alone ordered their crews to take the men aboard, over their subordinates' objection that the ships would be overloaded and lost. Wu Can answered:

「船敗，當俱死耳！人窮，奈何棄之。」[1]

The record concludes: 「粲、淵所活者百餘人」[1] — "Those whom Can and Yuan saved numbered over a hundred men."

So the credit is shared: both Wu Can and Huang Yuan gave the order, and the total saved was more than a hundred.

q: A soldier who went out and never came back was treated as a deserter, and his wife and children were made government slaves. His wife protested everywhere without success. Which Commandant of Justice eventually discovered that the soldier had been murdered for money by a man from his own camp, and who was the murderer?
reply:
The official was **Gao Rou (高柔)**, then Commandant of Justice (廷尉) of Wei, and the man he exposed was **Jiao Ziwen (焦子文)**, a soldier of Dou Li's own camp. The whole case is told in Gao Rou's biography in the Wei section of the *Sanguozhi*.

A soldier of the Protector-Army camp, Dou Li (竇禮), went out and did not come back. The camp treated him as a deserter and had him pursued: 「營以為亡，表言逐捕，沒其妻盈及男女為官奴婢」[1] — the camp took him for a fugitive, memorialized that he be pursued and arrested, and confiscated his wife Ying and their children as government slaves. Ying appealed repeatedly all the way to the provincial authorities and no one would look into it: 「盈連至州府，稱冤自訟，莫有省者。乃辭詣廷尉」[1]. So she stated her case to the Commandant of Justice.

Gao Rou asked how she knew her husband had not fled, and she answered that he had been orphaned and alone as a youth, had supported an old woman as his mother with great reverence, and loved his children, never leaving their side: 「夫少單特，養一老嫗為母，事甚恭謹，又哀兒女，撫視不離，非是輕狡不顧室家者也」[1]. Asked whether her husband had any enemies or money dealings, she said he had no enemies, but had once lent money to a fellow soldier of the same camp, Jiao Ziwen, and asked for it back without getting it: 「嘗出錢與同營士焦子文，求不得」[1].

Jiao Ziwen happened to be in prison at that moment on a minor charge: 「時子文適坐小事繫獄」[1]. Gao Rou questioned him about whether he had ever borrowed money from anyone, and Jiao denied it: 「汝頗曾舉人錢不？」子文曰：「自以單貧，初不敢舉人錢物也。」[1] Gao Rou caught the change in his face: 「柔察子文色動，遂曰：『汝昔舉竇禮錢，何言不邪？』」[1]. Jiao, startled that the matter was out, answered incoherently: 「子文恠知事露，應對不次」[1]. Gao Rou then said, 「汝已殺禮，便宜早服」[1], and Jiao knocked his head on the ground and gave a full account of how he had killed Li and where he had buried him: 「子文於是叩頭，具首殺禮本末，埋藏處所」[1]. Officers and soldiers were sent to dig at the place named in his statement, and the body was found at once: 「柔便遣吏卒，承子文辭往掘禮，即得其屍」[1]. An edict restored Ying and her children to commoner status, and the case was circulated through the realm as a warning: 「詔書復盈母子為平民。班下天下，以禮為戒」[1].

As for the motive: the record gives the loan and Jiao's refusal to repay it, and gives his confession to the killing, but does not spell out in so many words why he killed Dou Li. From the unpaid debt to the man he killed, and from his lie about never having borrowed money, it can be inferred that the money was the reason — that is my reading of the two recorded facts, not something the text states.

q: An official of Shu-Han dreamed that a mulberry tree grew out of a well. The dream interpreter told him he would not live past forty-eight, and sure enough he died at forty-eight. Who was this official, and who interpreted the dream?
reply:
The official was He Zhi (何祗, courtesy name Junsu 君肃), and the dream interpreter was Zhao Zhi (赵直), whom the text calls a "dream diviner" (占夢).

The anecdote is not in Chen Shou's main text; it comes in Pei Songzhi's note to the biography of Yang Hong in Shu juan 11, quoted from the *Yibu Qijiu Zhuan Zaji* (《益部耆旧传杂记》):

「嘗夢井中生桑，以問占夢趙直，直曰：『桑非井中之物，會當移植；然桑字四十下八，君壽恐不過此。』祗笑言『得此足矣』。」[2]

"He once dreamed that a mulberry grew in a well, and asked the dream diviner Zhao Zhi about it. Zhao Zhi said: 'The mulberry is not a thing that belongs in a well; it will surely be transplanted. But the character *sang* (桑) is "forty" with "eight" below — I fear your lifespan will not exceed this.' He Zhi laughed and said, 'That is enough for me.'"

The same note records the outcome: 「轉祗為犍為。年四十八卒，如直所言。」[11] — "He Zhi was transferred to be Administrator of Jianwei. He died at the age of forty-eight, just as Zhao Zhi had said."

Chen Shou's main text mentions He Zhi only briefly, as a man Yang Hong took in and promoted: 「洪迎門下書佐何祗，有才策功幹，舉郡吏，數年為廣漢太守」[12], followed by 「是以西土咸服諸葛亮能盡時人之器用也」[12] — Yang Hong received He Zhi as a retainer clerk (門下書佐); because of his ability and energy he was recommended as a commandery official, and within a few years became Administrator of Guanghan; and for this the whole west admired Zhuge Liang's ability to make full use of the talents of the men of his time.

Zhao Zhi appears elsewhere in the *Sanguozhi* in the same role: Jiang Wan 「呼問占夢趙直」[13], and Wei Yan likewise 「延夢頭上生角，以問占夢趙直，直詐延曰」[15] — that is, for Wei Yan he lied to him about the meaning of the dream.

q: A man opened up wasteland at Yongxing and planted twenty-odd mu of rice. Just as it was ripening, a local claimed it as his own; the man simply let him have the rice, and when the county Chief wanted to punish the local, he even pleaded on his behalf. Who was this man?
reply:
The man was **Zhongli Mu (鍾離牧)**, courtesy name Zigan, a man of Shanyin in Kuaiji. The story is in his biography in the *Book of Wu*.

The *Sanguozhi* records: 「鍾離牧字子幹，會稽山陰人，漢魯相意七世孫也。少爰居永興，躬自墾田，種稻二十餘畝。臨熟，縣民有識認之。牧曰：“本以田荒，故墾之耳。”遂以稻與縣人。縣長聞之，召民繋獄，欲繩以法，牧為之請。」[1] — "Zhongli Mu, courtesy name Zigan, a man of Shanyin in Kuaiji, seventh-generation descendant of Zhongli Yi, Chancellor of Lu in the Han… In his youth he moved to Yongxing, where he personally opened up wasteland and planted over twenty mu of rice. As it neared ripening, a man of the county came to claim it. Mu said: 'I only cleared it because the land was waste.' So he gave the rice to the man. When the county Chief heard of it, he summoned the man and put him in prison, intending to punish him by law, and Mu pleaded on his behalf."

The Chief answered, 「君慕承宮，自行義事，僕為民主，當以法率下，何得寢公憲而從君邪？」[1] — Mu admired Cheng Gong and acted on his own sense of what was right, but the Chief, as the people's magistrate, had to lead them by law and could not set aside public statute to follow him. Mu replied, 「此是郡界，緣君意顧，故來蹔住。今以少稻而殺此民，何心復留？」[1] — he had only been staying there out of regard for the Chief, and had no heart to remain if a man were to be killed over a little rice. He then packed up to return to Shanyin, and the Chief, going in person to stop him, released the prisoner. The man, ashamed and frightened, 「率妻子舂所取稻得六十斛米，送還牧，牧閉門不受。民輸置道旁，莫有取者。牧由此發名。」[1] — brought his wife and children to hull the rice he had taken, getting sixty hu of rice, and returned it to Mu, who shut his door and refused it; the man left it by the roadside and no one took it. Mu became famous because of this.

The Chief's mention of Cheng Gong is explained by Pei Songzhi's note, which quotes the *Xu Han Shu*: 「宫字少子，琅邪人，尝在蒙阴山中耕种禾黍，临熟，人就认之，宫便推与而去，由是发名，位至左中郎将、侍中。」[2] — Cheng Gong, courtesy name Shaozi, a man of Langya, was farming grain in the Mengyin hills; when it neared ripening a man came to claim it, and Cheng Gong simply yielded it and left, becoming known by this, and rising to the offices of Left General of the Household Gentlemen and Palace Attendant.

Not everyone approved. Pei's commentary also cites Xu Zhong's judgment: a questioner proposed that Mu's conduct — 「犯而不校，又從而救之，直而不有，又還而不受」[6] — could be called benevolence and yielding, and Xu Zhong answered that Mu walked in the rules of a elder, but 「今牧犯而不校，還而不取，可以為難矣，未得為仁讓也」[6]: the petty man who claimed another's rice was 「不仁甚矣」, so Mu's yielding was 「讓非其義，所救非人」, and Xu Zhong adds, 「必不得已，二者何從？吾從孔子也。」[6] That is a recorded disagreement, not the verdict of the text itself; the biography simply ends the episode with Mu's fame.

q: One of Cao Cao's military-planning officers (junmou yuan) ran into Cao Zhi on a muddy road inside the palace gate at Ye after a rain. He neither made way nor saluted, and even argued with Cao Zhi that 'the king's envoy, however lowly, ranks above the feudal lords.' Who was he, and what did he later gain from this?
reply:
The man was **Han Xuan (韩宣), courtesy name Jingran (景然)**, a native of Bohai. The story comes from Pei Songzhi's commentary quoting the *Weilüe* (裴注引《魏略》), attached to the biography of Pei Qian; Pei Songzhi notes that Han Xuan's name does not appear in Chen Shou's main text at all — only the *Weilüe* preserves his biography [11].

According to the account, in the Jian'an period the Chancellor (Cao Cao) summoned Han Xuan and appointed him a **junmou yuan (軍謀掾)**, and he was living idly at Ye. One day, passing through the palace gate, he met the Marquis of Linzi (Cao Zhi, before his later enfeoffments) inside the **East Side Gate (東掖門)**: "時天新雨，地有泥潦。宣欲避之，閡潦不得去。乃以扇自障，住於道邊" [11]. Cao Zhi disliked that he neither withdrew nor saluted, so he halted his carriage and had an attendant ask what office Han Xuan held. Han Xuan answered, "丞相軍謀掾也" (a Chancellor's military-planning officer), and when Cao Zhi asked whether he could be so insolent to a liege marquis, Han Xuan replied with the *Spring and Autumn* principle: 「春秋之義，王人雖微，列于諸侯之上，未聞宰士而爲下士諸侯禮也」 [2]. Cao Zhi pressed further — as his father's subordinate, should he not show propriety to the son? Han Xuan answered that in ritual, "臣、子一例也" (minister and son are of one class), and that he was also the elder. Cao Zhi, finding him hard to refute, let him go, and then told the whole episode to the Crown Prince (i.e. Cao Pi), praising Han Xuan's argumentation [2].

**What he gained from it:** the memory of that exchange later saved him. In the Huangchu period, Han Xuan was a **Secretary of the Department (尚書郎)**, and once, for an official matter, was to be punished before the hall — already bound, with the rods made ready but not yet applied. Emperor Wen (Cao Pi), passing by in his carriage, asked who it was; on hearing "尚書郎勃海韓宣也," the emperor recalled what the Marquis of Linzi had once said and exclaimed, 「是子建所道韓宣邪！」— "This is the Han Xuan that Zilian spoke of!" — and **specially pardoned him and had him untied** [2]. The account adds the comic detail that Han Xuan had pre-emptively removed his trousers for the flogging in the cold, and once released, could not undo his loincloth's waistband, so he shuffled off as he was; the emperor watched him go and laughed, calling him "此家有瞻諦之士也" [2].

他的身份和相遇的经过，《魏略》记：「韓宣字景然，勃海人也。爲人短小。建安中，丞相召署軍謀掾，宂散在鄴。嘗於鄴出入宮，於東掖門內與臨菑侯植相遇。時天新雨，地有泥潦。宣欲避之，閡潦不得去。乃以扇自障，住於道邊。」[11] 建安年间丞相曹操召他署为军谋掾，闲散住在邺城；他在东掖门内与临菑侯曹植相遇，正逢刚下过雨、地上有泥水，他想避让却被积水挡住走不开，只好用扇子遮住自己停在路边。

冲突的经过是：曹植「嫌宣既不去，又不爲禮，乃駐車，使其常從問宣何官」，韩宣答「丞相軍謀掾也」；曹植问「應得唐突列侯否」，韩宣答「春秋之義，王人雖微，列于諸侯之上，未聞宰士而爲下士諸侯禮也」；曹植再问身为父亲的属吏见其子是否应有礼，韩宣答「於禮，臣、子一例也，而宣年又長」。最后「植知其枝柱難窮，乃釋去，具爲太子言，以爲辯」[2]——曹植辩不过他，放他走了，并把这件事详细讲给太子听，认为他善辩。这位太子从下文文帝追念此事看应是曹丕，这一点是据前后文推出的。

**他从这件事上得到的实际好处，是后来一次免罚。**《魏略》接着记：「黃初中，爲尚書郎，嘗以職事當受罰於殿前，已縛，束杖未行。文帝輦過，問：『此爲誰？』左右對曰：『尚書郎勃海韓宣也。』帝追念前臨菑侯所說，乃寤曰：『是子建所道韓宣邪！』特原之，遂解其縛。」[2] 黄初年间他做尚书郎，因职事要在殿前受罚，已经绑好、刑杖还未落下，魏文帝乘车经过，问是谁，左右答是尚书郎勃海韩宣，文帝想起当年临菑侯说过的话，醒悟说「这就是曹子建所说的韩宣啊」，于是特别宽免、解开绑绳。当时天很冷，韩宣因将要受杖已先脱了裤子、只缠着裤衩被反绑着，获释后裤衩腰带解不下来，就这样快步离去，文帝目送他，笑道「此家有瞻諦之士也」[2]。赦免的直接理由，原文写明是文帝追念曹植先前所说，这条因果是记载本身给的，不是推出来的。

q: Which Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant of Wu got drunk and collapsed at the banquet Sun Hao held for Ding Zhong on his return from an embassy to Jin, and was beheaded in the hall on Sun Hao's orders? In which year?
reply:
**王蕃 (Wang Fan), in 甘露二年 — 266 AD.**

The man was Wang Fan 王蕃, styled Yongyuan 永元 of Lujiang. He was a 散騎中常侍 (Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant) under Sun Hao. The account is in the *Wu Shu*, in the biography of Wang Fan (with Lou Xuan, He Shao, Wei Zhao, Hua He).

The main record: 「甘露二年，丁忠使晉還，皓大會群臣，蕃沉醉頓伏。皓疑而不悅，舉蕃出外。頃之請還，酒亦不解。蕃性有威嚴，行止自若，皓大怒，呵左右於殿下斬之。衛將軍滕牧、征西將軍留平請，不能得。」[1]

(Translation: In the second year of Ganlu, Ding Zhong returned from his embassy to Jin; Sun Hao held a great assembly of his ministers, and Wang Fan, dead drunk, fell prostrate. Sun Hao grew suspicious and displeased, and had him carried outside. After a while Wang Fan asked to return, his drunkenness still not cleared. Wang Fan was by nature dignified, and bore himself as usual; Sun Hao flew into a rage and ordered his attendants to behead him below the hall. The General of the Guard Teng Mu and the General of the West Liu Ping pleaded for him, but could not obtain a pardon.)

Earlier in the same biography we are told he had served as 散騎中常侍 alongside He Shao, Xue Ying and Yu Si, and that under Sun Hao he re-entered court as 常侍, sharing office with Wan Yu [11][14].

On the year: the text says 甘露二年, which the Wu (Sun Hao) calendar converts to **266 AD** [era]. Note the ambiguity of the era name: Sun Hao's Wu also used 甘露, and the same two characters were used by Cao Wei (256–260) — here it is the Wu one.

One caveat on the sources. Pei Songzhi quotes a different version: the *Jiangbiao Zhuan* says Sun Hao, misled by shamans, went west to Wuchang intending to move the capital, and killed Wang Fan at a banquet by asking him the meaning of "archery does not stress piercing the target"; it notes 「此與本傳不同」[5]. Pei Songzhi's own note sides with the main biography's account of the Ding Zhong banquet, and argues that the *Wu Lu*'s story (in which Wang Fan mocks Wan Yu as left chancellor) is inconsistent, since Ding Zhong came back from the north in spring of that year while Wan Yu did not become chancellor until autumn [5]. So the version naming the Ding Zhong banquet and the hall beheading is the one given by the *Sanguozhi* main text.

那个在丁忠出使晋国回来后、孙皓大会群臣的酒席上醉倒、被孙皓下令在殿上斩首的吴国散骑常侍，是王蕃；王蕃传把这件事记在甘露二年，据年号换算为公元 266 年。

据王蕃传，王蕃字永元，庐江人[11]。孙休即位后，他与贺邵、薛莹、虞汜同为散骑中常侍，都加授驸马都尉；孙皓初年又入朝任常侍，与万彧同官[11][14]。后来陆凯上疏时称他为「常侍王蕃」[19]。

本传正文记这件事： 「甘露二年，丁忠使晉還，皓大會群臣，蕃沉醉頓伏。皓疑而不悅，舉蕃出外。頃之請還，酒亦不解。蕃性有威嚴，行止自若，皓大怒，呵左右於殿下斬之。衛將軍滕牧、征西將軍留平請，不能得。」[1] 大意是：丁忠出使晋国回来，孙皓大会群臣，王蕃喝得大醉伏倒在地；孙皓起疑、很不高兴，命人把他抬出去，不久他请求回席，酒仍未醒，举止仍如平常，孙皓大怒，令左右在殿下把他斩了，卫将军滕牧、征西将军留平求情也没能救下。

同一段的裴注里另有两种说法。裴注引《江表传》说：孙皓听信巫史之言，认为建业宫不利，于是西巡武昌并有迁都之意，怕群臣不从，便大设宴会，问王蕃「射不主皮，為力不同科」是什么意思，王蕃思索未答，就在殿上被斩，裴松之指出「此與本傳不同」[5]。裴注又引《吴录》说：孙皓每逢宴会，趁酒酣就让侍臣嘲谑公卿取乐；万彧做了左丞相后，王蕃嘲讽他「羊質虎皮」等语[5]。裴松之按：「臣松之按本傳云丁忠使晉還，皓為大會，於會中殺蕃，檢忠從北還在此年之春，彧時尚未為丞相，至秋乃為相耳。吳錄所言為乖互不同。」[5]

由此看，把此事系在丁忠出使归来那次大会、王蕃被斩于殿上，是《三国志》本传正文的说法；《江表传》的版本（因答问而见杀）与之不同，裴松之也指出《吴录》的说法与时间不合。

q: Who had the courtesy name Wenze?
reply:
In the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* two men bore the courtesy name Wenze (文則) — one a Wei general, one a Wu official.

**Yu Jin (于禁), style Wenze**, a Wei general from Juping in Taishan Commandery. His biography opens: 「于禁字文則，泰山鉅平人也。」[1] He attached himself to Bao Xin when the Yellow Turbans rose — 「黃巾起，鮑信招合徒衆，禁附從焉」[1] — and later served Cao Cao, being counted among the foremost generals of the time: 「太祖建茲武功，而時之良將，五子爲先。」[8] He was noted for strict discipline: 「而禁持軍嚴整，得賊財物，無所私入」[6]. In 建安二十四年 Cao Cao, then in Chang'an, sent Cao Ren against Guan Yu at Fan and sent Yu Jin to assist him; after autumn rains flooded the Han River and his seven armies were lost, 「禁遂降，惟龐德不屈節而死」[2]. Cao Cao lamented: 「吾知禁三十年，何意臨危處難，反不如龐德邪！」[2]. Later Emperor Wen (Cao Pi) had Yu Jin go north to pay respects at Gaoling, where scenes of Guan Yu's victory, Pang De's fury and Yu Jin's surrender had been painted in advance; on seeing them, 「慚恚發病薨」, and he was given the posthumous title recorded as 「諡禁曰厲侯」[2]. Chen Shou's verdict: 「于禁最號毅重，然弗克其終。」[8]

**Wu Fan (吳範), style Wenze**, a man of Shangyu in Kuaiji Commandery: 「吳範字文則，會稽上虞人也。以治曆數知風氣聞於郡中。」[9] He attached himself to Sun Quan and would calculate and report on every portent: 「會孫權起於東南，範委身服事，每有災祥，輒推數言狀。其術多效，遂以顯名。」[9] Sun Quan made him Commandant of Cavalry and put him in charge of the Grand Astrologers (騎都尉，領太史令), but Wu Fan kept his methods secret and did not tell Sun Quan the essentials: 「範祕惜其術，不以至要語權。權由是恨之。」[14] He died of illness in 黃武五年, and his household line came to an end: 「黃武五年，範病卒。長子先死，少子尚幼，於是業絕。」[16]

So 由此看, if the text you have gives only the courtesy name "Wenze," you have to judge by context: a Wei general is Yu Jin, a Wu diviner is Wu Fan — this is my inference from the two biographies, not something the *Records* states.

q: Who was the man that Kuan Yü's troops called the 'White Horse General' (Baima jiangjun)?
reply:
**Pang De (龐德, styled Lingming 令明)** of the Wei army — the officer who shot Guan Yu in the forehead at Fancheng in 219 and was afterwards captured and killed by him.

The nickname is explained in Pang De's biography in the *Wei Shu*: 「後親與羽交戰，射羽中額。時德常乘白馬，羽軍謂之白馬將軍，皆憚之。」[3] — "Later he personally fought Guan Yu and shot him in the forehead. At that time De habitually rode a white horse; Guan Yu's troops called him the 'White Horse General,' and all of them feared him."

The context: Pang De had originally served Ma Teng and Ma Chao, then followed Zhang Lu, and surrendered to Cao Cao when Cao Cao took Hanzhong; Cao Cao, who had long heard of his ferocity, made him General of Righteousness (立義將軍) and Marquis of the Guammen Pavilion [2]. Before Fancheng, since his elder brother was on Liu Bei's side in Hanzhong, the officers there suspected him, and he declared: 「我受國恩，義在效死。我欲身自擊羽。今年我不殺羽，羽當殺我。」[3] After the Han River flooded and drowned Yu Jin's seven armies, Pang De fought on the dike, executed officers who wanted to surrender, and when his arrows were gone and his boat capsized he was taken. He refused to kneel and cursed Guan Yu — 「竪子，何謂降也！」[3] — saying he would rather be a ghost of the state than a general of the rebels: 「我寧為國家鬼，不為賊將也。」[5] — and was killed. Cao Cao wept for him and enfeoffed two of his sons; Cao Pi later gave him the posthumous title 壯侯, "the Valiant Marquis" [5]. The *Weilüe* adds that his cousin (裴注引《魏略》: 從兄, not brother) Pang Rou was then in Shu [12], which is the relative Guan Yu referred to when urging him to surrender.

One thing worth separating out, since the same colour appears twice in the sources: the phrase "white horse" is also attached to Gongsun Zan, whose cavalry were styled 白馬義從 and of whom the Wuhuan said 「當避白馬」[14]. That is a separate matter and a different wording — the title "White Horse General," as used of Guan Yu's opponent, belongs to Pang De alone.

关羽军称之为"白马将军"的，是魏将**庞德**（字令明）。此名出自庞德本人的传记：庞德与关羽亲自交战，射中关羽额头，而他常骑白马，所以关羽军中这样称呼他，并且都畏惧他。

据《三国志·魏书·庞德传》，庞德是南安狟道人，早年随马腾、马超，后来随马超奔汉中依张鲁，曹操平定汉中时随众投降；曹操一向听说他骁勇，任命他为立义将军，封关门亭侯，食邑三百户[2]。樊城之战前，因他的兄长在汉中，樊城下的诸将对他颇有怀疑，庞德说：「我受國恩，義在效死。我欲身自擊羽。今年我不殺羽，羽當殺我。」[3]

关于"白马将军"这个称呼，原文是：「後親與羽交戰，射羽中額。時德常乘白馬，羽軍謂之白馬將軍，皆憚之。」[3] 当时曹仁派庞德驻在樊城北十里，连日大雨、汉水暴涨，庞德与诸将避水登堤；关羽乘船来攻，庞德披甲持弓，箭不虚发，将军董衡、部曲将董超等想投降，都被他收斩[3]。箭尽后短兵接战，船覆被擒，「立而不跪」[3]。关羽劝降说「卿兄在漢中，我欲以卿為將，不早降何為？」[3]，庞德骂道：「竪子，何謂降也！」[3] 又说：「我寧為國家鬼，不為賊將也。」[5]，于是被关羽所杀[5]。曹操听说后为他流泪，封他两个儿子为列侯；曹丕即王位后派使者到庞德墓前赐谥，策文称「謚曰壯侯」，又赐其子庞会等四人关内侯爵位[5]。庞德之死，在关羽传里记于建安二十四年（先主为汉中王、关羽攻曹仁于樊那一年），与于禁投降一同记作「羽又斬將軍龐德」[4]。

补充一点记载上的差异：关羽劝降时说的是"卿兄在漢中"，而裴注引《魏略》说「德從兄名柔，時在蜀」[12]——即那个亲属是庞德的从兄庞柔，一作在汉中，一作在蜀，两处说法并不完全一致，这里并列说明，不作裁定。

q: The Weilüe mentions a man called 'Nukou' ('Slave Bandit'). Who was he, and which other generals' alternative names are given in the same passage?
reply:
"Nukou" (奴寇, "Slave Bandit") was an alternative name of Zang Ba (臧霸). The same *Weilüe* passage also gives alternative names for three other generals: Sun Guan, Wu Dun and Yin Li.

The *Weilüe* note appended to Zang Ba's biography in the *Wei shu* reads:

「《魏略》曰：霸一名奴寇。孫觀名嬰子。吳敦名黯奴。尹禮名盧兒。」[1]

So, according to the *Weilüe*: Zang Ba was also named Nukou (奴寇); Sun Guan was named Yingzi (嬰子); Wu Dun was named Annu (黯奴); and Yin Li was named Lu'er (盧兒). Four men's alternative names appear together in this one passage.

Zang Ba, styled Xuangao (宣高), has his own biography. 「文帝即王位，遷鎮東將軍，進爵武安鄉侯，都督青州諸軍事。及踐阼，進封開陽侯，徙封良成侯。」[20] He then campaigned with Cao Xiu and defeated Lü Fan at Dongpu, was summoned as Bearer of the Gilded Mace (執金吾) and ranked as Special Advance (特進); after Emperor Ming ascended the throne his fief was increased by five hundred households, to three thousand five hundred in all; 「薨，謚曰威侯。」[20]

Sun Guan also has his own biography. The *Wei shu* quoted in Pei Songzhi's note says: 「《魏書》曰：孫觀字仲台，泰山人。與臧霸俱起，討黃巾，拜騎都尉。太祖破呂布，使霸招觀兄弟，皆厚遇之。」[24] He fought alongside Zang Ba and often led the assault, and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Lüdu Pavilion; later 「拜觀偏將軍，遷青州刺史。從徵孫權於濡須口，假節。攻權，為流矢所中，傷左足，力戰不顧，太祖勞之曰：「將軍被創深重，而猛氣益奮，不當為國愛身乎？」轉振威將軍，創甚，遂卒。」[24]

Wu Dun and Yin Li have no biographies of their own; the *Weilüe* gives their alternative names in the same note [1].

The note then continues with separate events. In the twenty-fourth year of Jian'an, Zang Ba sent a detached force to Luoyang; when 太祖 died, Zang Ba's troops and the Qingzhou soldiers thought the realm would fall into chaos and all beat drums and left on their own; Emperor Wen made Cao Xiu supervisor of Qingzhou and Xuzhou, and Zang Ba told Cao Xiu that if he were given ten thousand foot and horse he could sweep the south of the Yangtze; Cao Xiu reported this, and Emperor Wen, suspecting Zang Ba's army had earlier departed without orders, went on an eastern tour and took away Zang Ba's troops when he came to court: 「建安二十四年，霸遣別軍在洛。會太祖崩，霸所部及青州兵，以為天下將亂，皆鳴鼓擅去。文帝即位，以曹休都督青、徐，霸謂休曰：『國家未肯聽霸耳！若假霸步騎萬人，必能橫行江表。』休言之於帝，帝疑霸軍前擅去，今意壯乃爾！遂東巡，因霸來朝而奪其兵。」[1]

q: Who was the Marquis of Panyu, and for what achievement was he given that title?
reply:
The Marquis of Panyu (番禺侯) was **Lü Dai (吕岱)**, style name Dinggong (定公), a general of Wu. The *who* index confirms the title belonged to him — his alternative appellation in the record is precisely "番禺侯."

The enfeoffment came as a reward for crushing the revolt of **Shi Hui (士徽)** in Jiaozhi. After the Administrator of Jiaozhi, Shi Xie, died, Sun Quan made Shi Xie's son Shi Hui Acting General of An Yuan and concurrent Administrator of Jiuzhen, while sending Chen Shi to replace Shi Xie; Shi Hui refused the order and raised troops at the sea port to block Dai Liang. Lü Dai asked for permission to punish him and led 3,000 men by sea. He caught Shi Hui unprepared; Shi Hui, terrified, came out with six of his brothers, stripped to the waist, to receive him. Lü Dai beheaded them and sent the heads off. Shi Hui's chief generals Gan Li and Huan Zhi then attacked Lü Dai with officials and commoners, and Lü Dai beat them off.

It was this victory that earned him the title: 「徽聞岱至，果大震怖，不知所出，即率兄弟六人肉袒迎岱。岱皆斬送其首，徽大將甘醴，桓治等率吏民攻岱，岱奮擊大破之，進封番禺侯」[1] — "Hearing that Dai had arrived, Hui was indeed greatly shocked and frightened, not knowing what to do; he at once led six of his brothers, bare-bodied, to welcome Dai. Dai beheaded them all and sent off their heads. Hui's chief generals Gan Li, Huan Zhi and others led officials and people to attack Dai; Dai struck out fiercely and routed them, and was advanced in fief as Marquis of Panyu."

Several points worth noting. First, this was a promotion, not a first enfeoffment: earlier, in the first year of Yankang (延康元年, 220 CE), after capturing the bandit Wang Jin, he had already been made 「安南將軍，假節，封都鄉侯」[9] — General Who Calms the South, with the staff of authority, and Marquis of Duxiang. Second, the sequel: right after the enfeoffment, Lü Dai abolished Guangzhou and restored Jiaozhi circuit as before, then went on to subdue Jiuzhen, and Sun Quan, commending his merit, further promoted him to General Who Guards the South — 「權嘉其功，進拜鎮南將軍」[1]. Third, the fuller narrative of the Shi Hui affair, with the killing of Huan Lin and the role of Shi Kuang, appears in the biography of Shi Xie [3]; but the granting of the title of Marquis of Panyu is recorded in Lü Dai's own biography.

番禺侯是吴将吕岱（字定公），这个爵位是进封来的，进封的直接原因是他讨平了士徽在交州的叛乱。

吕岱其人，本传开头写得很清楚：「呂岱字定公，廣陵海陵人也」[4]，本传在《吴书》中。事情的经过是：交阯太守士燮死后，孙权安排后事，「交阯太守士燮卒，權以燮子徽為安遠將軍，領九真太守，以校尉陳時代燮」[1]；士徽不肯从命，「徽不承命，舉兵戍海口以拒良等」[1]。吕岱于是上疏请讨，「岱於是上疏請討徽罪，督兵三千人晨夜浮海」[1]，走海路突袭。他事先判断士徽不会料到吴军骤至——「今徽雖懷逆計，未虞吾之卒至」[1]——士徽果然惊惶出迎，接着被杀，其部将反攻又被击破，吕岱因此进封番禺侯：

「徽聞岱至，果大震怖，不知所出，即率兄弟六人肉袒迎岱。岱皆斬送其首，徽大將甘醴，桓治等率吏民攻岱，岱奮擊大破之，進封番禺侯」[1]

封侯之后，他「於是除廣州，復為交州如故」[1]，又进军九真，孙权嘉其功，「權嘉其功，進拜鎮南將軍」[1]。

有两点补充。第一，番禺侯不是他第一次封侯：本传在叙述次序上更早的一段记，延康元年他接替步骘任交州刺史，擒送贼帅王金之后「遷安南將軍，假節，封都鄉侯」[9]。由此看，本传用「進封」二字、且此前已有都乡侯之封，番禺侯应是进爵而非初封——这是从这两条记载推出的，不是原文直接下的断语。第二，士徽之事的详细经过另见《士燮传》：士徽拒迎戴良时，交阯人桓邻叩头劝谏而被笞杀，「交阯桓鄰，燮舉吏也，叩頭諫徽使迎良，徽怒，笞殺鄰」[3]；吕岱又用与己有旧交的士匡去劝说士徽，「壹子中郎將匡與岱有舊，岱署匡師友從事，先移書交阯，告喻禍福，又遣匡見徽」[3]。这些是[1]所记同一事件的前后细节。至于番禺侯这一封号本身，见于吕岱本传的记载。

q: Why was Wei Zhao put to death by Sun Hao?
reply:
Wei Zhao (written in the *Sanguozhi* as "Wei Yao," courtesy name Hongsi) was thrown into prison by Sun Hao and then put to death. The text dates the imprisonment to the second year of Fenghuang, i.e. AD 273: 「遂積前後嫌忿，收曜付獄，是歲鳳凰二年也」[3] — "So he accumulated his resentment from earlier and later, and had Yao arrested and handed over to the prison; this year was the second year of Fenghuang." The execution is recorded after this, with no separate year given. The reasons the biography gives are quite clear, item by item.

First, blunt speech that offended Sun Hao. After Sun Hao came to the throne, he enfeoffed Wei Yao as Marquis of Gaoling Pavilion, promoted him to Supervisor of the Palace Secretariat, and, after that office was abolished, made him Palace Attendant while he continued to serve concurrently as Left State Historian. At that time, places everywhere flattered Sun Hao's wishes and repeatedly reported auspicious omens; Sun Hao asked him about it, and he answered: 「此人家筐篋中物耳」[3] — "These are just the things in people's baskets and boxes." Sun Hao then wanted to make a "Benji" (annals) for his father Sun He, and Wei Yao insisted that since Sun He had never ascended the throne, it should be called a "zhuan" (biography): 「曜執以和不登帝位，宜名為傳」[3] — "Yao held firmly that because He did not ascend the imperial throne, it should be titled a biography." Such things were more than one instance: 「如是者非一，漸見責怒」[3] — "Things like this were not one or two, and he gradually came to be reprimanded and angered."

Second, he would not obey orders at drinking banquets. Every time Sun Hao feasted, the gathering lasted all day, and everyone seated, whether able to drink or not, was held to a limit of seven sheng: 「雖不悉入口，皆澆灌取盡」[3] — "Even if it did not all go down his throat, he would pour it down to finish it." Wei Yao by nature drank no more than two sheng; at first, when he was treated with special courtesy, he was often given a reduction, and sometimes tea was secretly given to him in place of wine — 「至於寵衰，更見逼強，輒以為罪」[3] — "but when the favor declined, he was all the more forced, and it was taken as a crime." Sun Hao also had his attendants, after drinking, press and humiliate the high ministers, taking mockery and the exposure of private faults as amusement; Wei Yao thought this 「外相毀傷，內長尤恨」[3] — "outwardly injures one another and inwardly breeds deeper resentment" — was no good thing, and so only raised questions on the meaning of the classics. Sun Hao therefore judged that he 「不承用詔命，意不忠盡」[3] — "did not accept and carry out the imperial commands, and his heart was not wholly loyal" — and so accumulated his grievances and had him imprisoned [3].

After entering prison, Wei Yao submitted a statement in his own defense, saying he was writing the *Dongji* and had also composed the *Guanzhi Xun* and *Bianshi Ming*, one roll each, which he wished to present, hoping thereby to gain pardon [11][12]; Sun Hao instead blamed the dirtiness of his manuscript, 「又以詰曜」[13] — "and again interrogated Yao about it." Hua He repeatedly submitted memorials to save him, comparing Wei Yao to Sima Qian of the Han: 「今曜在吳，亦漢之史遷也」[13] — "Now Yao in Wu is the Han's Sima Qian," and noting that he was already seventy, asked that he 「赦其一等之罪，為終身徒，使成書業」[14] — "be pardoned one degree of his crime and made a lifelong convict, so that he might complete his literary work." Sun Hao refused: 「皓不許，遂誅曜，徙百家零陵。子隆，亦有文學也。」[14] — "Hao did not permit it, and so executed Yao and moved a hundred families of his household to Lingling. His son Long also had literary talent."

From this it appears that Wei Yao's death was the result of his repeated blunt speech and his refusal to obey orders, together with the grievances that accumulated between him and Sun Hao — but this causal link is one the text itself states ("積前後嫌忿," "he accumulated his resentment from earlier and later"), not merely my inference. As for whether Sun Hao treated his ministers this way across the board, the evidence here is only this one biography of Wei Yao, and it should not be extended from this single case to others.

韦昭（《三国志》写作“韦曜”，字弘嗣）是被孙皓下狱后处死的，时在凤凰二年（公元273年）[凤皇2年=273]。直接的导火索是两件事触怒了孙皓，加上平日积怨，最终送了命。

此外还有宴饮之事。孙皓每次宴饮终日，座中人无论能否喝酒一律以七升为限，喝不下也要浇灌喝尽；韦昭平素不过二升，起初受礼遇时还为他裁减，甚至暗中赐茶代酒，「至於寵衰，更見逼強，輒以為罪」[3]。孙皓又让侍臣在酒后诘难折辱公卿、揭人隐私为乐，韦昭认为这样「外相毀傷，內長尤恨」不好，只就经义发问而已，孙皓便认为他「不承用詔命，意不忠盡」，于是「積前後嫌忿，收曜付獄」[3]，这是凤凰二年的事。

入狱后韦昭上书自陈，说自己正在撰《洞纪》《官职训》《辩释名》等书，希望得到宽免；孙皓反而责怪他的书稿污损，又加责问[13]。华覈接连上疏营救，把韦昭比作汉代的司马迁，说「今曜在吳，亦漢之史遷也」，并称他年已七十，请求「赦其一等之罪，為終身徒，使成書業」[13]。孙皓不准：「皓不許，遂誅曜，徙百家零陵。子隆，亦有文學也。」[14]

所以，据原文，孙皓杀韦昭不是单一罪名：拒附祥瑞、坚持不为孙和立“纪”，加上不肯在酒宴上奉命折辱公卿，被认定“不承用诏命、意不忠尽”，新旧嫌怨累积，终于下狱处死，家属百家被迁往零陵。由此看，韦昭之死与孙皓晚年猜忌、拒谏、以史官直笔为忤的作风是一致的，但因果只是推断；原文只记了上述事实与孙皓的处置结果。

韦昭（《三国志》中写作“韦曜”，字弘嗣）是被孙皓下狱后处死的。原文把下狱一事系于凤凰二年，即公元273年：「遂積前後嫌忿，收曜付獄，是歲鳳凰二年也」[3]；诛杀记在其后，未另标年份。致死的缘由，传里逐条写得很清楚。

一是触怒孙皓的直言。孙皓即位后，封韦曜为高陵亭侯，迁中书仆射，官职裁省后改任侍中，常领左国史。当时各地迎合孙皓之意屡报祥瑞，孙皓拿这事问他，他答：「此人家筐篋中物耳」[3]。孙皓想为父亲孙和作“纪”，韦曜坚持孙和没有登上帝位，应称“传”：「曜執以和不登帝位，宜名為傳」[3]。这类事不止一件，「如是者非一，漸見責怒」[3]。

二是宴饮中不肯奉命。孙皓每次宴饮无不终日，座中人不论能否饮酒一律以七升为限，「雖不悉入口，皆澆灌取盡」[3]。韦曜平素饮酒不过二升，起初受特别礼遇时还常为他裁减，有时暗中赐茶代酒，「至於寵衰，更見逼強，輒以為罪」[3]。孙皓又在酒后让侍臣诘难折辱公卿，以嘲弄、揭发隐私为乐；韦曜认为这样「外相毀傷，內長尤恨」，不是好事，所以只就经义言论发问而已。孙皓因此认为他「不承用詔命，意不忠盡」，于是积怨将他下狱[3]。

入狱后韦曜上书自陈，说自己在撰《洞纪》，又作《官职训》《辩释名》各一卷，想上表进呈，希望以此求免[11][12]；孙皓反而责怪他的书稿污损，「又以詰曜」[13]。华覈接连上疏营救，把韦曜比作汉代的司马迁：「今曜在吳，亦漢之史遷也」，并称他年已七十，请求「赦其一等之罪，為終身徒，使成書業」[14]。孙皓不准：「皓不許，遂誅曜，徙百家零陵。子隆，亦有文學也。」[14]

由此看，韦曜之死是他屡次直言、不肯奉诏与孙皓之间嫌怨累积的结果——这层因果原文自己已经点明（“積前後嫌忿”），不是我的推测；但至于孙皓是否对臣下一概如此，本次所据仅韦曜一传的记载，不宜由这一例推及其他。

q: What happened when Zhuge Liang used the Empty Fort Strategy at Yangping to scare off Sima Yi?
reply:
The main text of the *Sanguozhi* contains no record of Zhuge Liang using an "empty fort" at Yangping to scare off Sima Yi; the story appears only in a book called Guo Chong's *Sanshi*, quoted in Pei Songzhi's commentary, and the rebuttal that immediately follows in that commentary rejects it.

As recorded in the *Sanshi* quoted in the commentary: Zhuge Liang was stationed at Yangping and 「遣魏延諸軍並兵東下，亮惟留萬人守城」[1] — "he sent Wei Yan and the other armies to combine forces and move east, and Zhuge Liang kept only ten thousand men to hold the city." Sima Yi (Jin Xuandi) 「率二十萬眾拒亮」[1] — "led two hundred thousand troops to oppose Zhuge Liang" — but his route crossed with Wei Yan's army and he came straight on ahead, 「當亮六十里所」[1] — "about sixty li from Zhuge Liang" — and his scouts reported that Zhuge Liang had few troops and was weak in the city [1]. Zhuge Liang knew Sima Yi was about to arrive and had already drawn close, and 「欲前赴延軍，相去又遠，回跡反追，勢不相及，將士失色，莫知其計」[1] — "he wanted to go forward to join Wei Yan's army, but the distance was too great; to turn back and pursue, the situation would not allow it, and his officers and men turned pale, not knowing what plan to use." Zhuge Liang remained calm as ever, and 「敕軍中皆臥旗息鼓，不得妄出菴幔，又令大開四城門，埽地卻洒」[1] — "he ordered the army to lay down its banners and silence its drums, not to come out of their tents without cause, and further ordered all four city gates thrown open and the ground swept and sprinkled." Sima Yi had always considered Zhuge Liang steady and cautious, and now suddenly seeing him show weakness, 「疑其有伏兵，於是引軍北趣山」[1] — "he suspected an ambush and therefore led his army north to the mountains." At mealtime the next day Zhuge Liang clapped his hands and laughed to his staff, saying: 「司馬懿必謂吾怯，將有彊伏，循山走矣。」[1] — "Sima Yi must think I am timid, and that there is a strong ambush, so he has gone off along the mountains." The scouts and patrols came back and reported that it was just as Zhuge Liang had said; when Sima Yi later learned the truth, 「深以為恨」[1] — "he deeply regretted it."

The rebuttal immediately following this passage in the commentary says: Yangping is in Hanzhong; when Zhuge Liang first camped at Yangping, Sima Yi was still Inspector of Jingzhou, stationed at Wancheng, and 「至曹真死後，始與亮於關中相抗禦耳」[1] — "only after Cao Zhen's death did he begin to oppose Zhuge Liang in the Guanzhong region" — and before and after that 「無復有於陽平交兵事」[1] — "there was no further affair of armies clashing at Yangping." Moreover, 「就如沖言，宣帝既舉二十萬眾，已知亮兵少力弱，若疑其有伏兵，正可設防持重，何至便走乎」[1] — "even granting Guo Chong's account, since Xuandi had raised two hundred thousand troops and already knew Zhuge Liang's soldiers were few and weak, if he suspected an ambush he could simply have set up defenses and acted with caution; why would he just flee?" The rebuttal also cites the *Wei Yan zhuan*: 「延每隨亮出，輒欲請精兵萬人，與亮異道會于潼關，亮制而不許」[20] — "whenever Wei Yan went out with Zhuge Liang, he always wanted to request ten thousand picked troops and meet Zhuge Liang by a different route at Tongguan, but Zhuge Liang restrained him and would not permit it." Zhuge Liang would not even let Wei Yan independently command ten thousand men, 「豈得如沖言，頓使將重兵在前，而以輕弱自守乎」[20] — "how could it be, as Guo Chong says, that he suddenly let him lead heavy troops in front while he himself with weak, light forces held the defense?" On this basis the rebuttal concludes 「此書舉引皆虛」[20] — "the citations in this book are all false."

From this it can be seen: this story cannot be found in the main text of the *Sanguozhi*; it appears only in Guo Chong's *Sanshi* as quoted in Pei Songzhi's commentary, and that commentary's rebuttal points out on three grounds — time, place, and plausibility — that it is unreliable. To speak of that "empty fort" at Yangping, one can only say it is a single account preserved in the commentary, not a record of the *Sanguozhi*.

q: In the Battle of Bowang, how did Zhuge Liang set the fire ambush against Xiahou Dun?
reply:
The question's premise comes from the novel, not from the *Sanguozhi*: the histories do not give the Bowang fire ambush to Zhuge Liang. They record it as Liu Bei's own ruse.

Liu Bei's biography: after Cao Cao defeated Yuan Shao, he attacked Liu Bei from the south; Liu Bei contacted Liu Biao, who welcomed him as an honored guest, gave him troops and stationed him at Xinye, then sent him to hold off Xiahou Dun and Yu Jin at Bowang: 「使拒夏侯惇、于禁等於博望。久之，先主設伏兵，一旦自燒屯偽遁，惇等追之，為伏兵所破。」[1] (He was sent to resist Xiahou Dun, Yu Jin and others at Bowang. After a long time, the Former Lord set hidden troops; one morning he himself burned his camp and feigned flight; Dun and the others pursued him and were broken by the hidden troops.)

Li Dian's biography gives the other side of the same engagement: 「劉表使劉備北侵，至葉，太祖遣典從夏侯惇拒之。備一旦燒屯去，惇率諸軍追擊之，典曰：『賊無故退，疑必有伏。南道狹窄，草木深，不可追也。』惇不聽，與於禁追之，典留守。惇等果入賊伏里，戰不利，典往救，備望見救至，乃散退。」[19] (Liu Biao sent Liu Bei to invade north; he reached Ye, and the Grand Progenitor sent Li Dian to accompany Xiahou Dun against him. One morning Bei burned his camp and left; Dun led the armies in pursuit. Li Dian said, "The enemy retreats without cause; I suspect there must be an ambush. The southern road is narrow, the grass and trees are thick—we must not pursue." Dun would not listen and pursued with Yu Jin; Li Dian stayed behind. Dun and the others indeed entered the enemy's ambush and the fighting went badly; Li Dian went to the rescue, and Bei, seeing the relief arrive, dispersed and withdrew.)

So as recorded the sequence is: Liu Bei burned his own camp, feigned flight, drew Xiahou Dun (and Yu Jin) into pursuit along a narrow, wooded road, and sprang the hidden troops—with Li Dian's warning ignored. Li Dian stayed behind, then came to the rescue, and Liu Bei withdrew on seeing the relief force.

Zhuge Liang's biography [20] opens with his origins, his self-comparison to Guan Zhong and Yue Yi, and his friendship with Cui Zhouping and Xu Shu; it contains no Bowang fire ambush. The materials contain no record of Zhuge Liang at Bowang at all. The episode in which Zhuge Liang lays the fire trap at Bowang Slope is the novel's, which moves the credit from Liu Bei to Zhuge Liang.

q: What is the story of Kuan Yü killing Ts'ai Yang at Ku-ch'eng?
reply:
In the *Sanguozhi* the killing of Cai Yang is recorded, but the killer is **Liu Bei**, not Guan Yu; and the sources give no place called Gucheng in connection with it. The story of Guan Yu slaying Cai Yang at Gucheng is not what these records say.

What the records do say about Guan Yu: in 建安五年 Cao Cao took him captive on the eastern campaign, and after he killed Yan Liang at Baima he left Cao Cao and went back to Liu Bei: 「羽盡封其所賜，拜書告辭，而奔先主於袁軍」[1]. His own biography records nothing about Cai Yang, and nothing about a Gucheng.

Cai Yang's death stands in Liu Bei's biography, in the Runan period: first 「關羽亡歸先主」[2], then 「紹遣先主將本兵復至汝南，與賊龔都等合，眾數千人。曹公遣蔡陽擊之，為先主所殺」[2] — Cai Yang was sent by Cao Cao against Liu Bei and Gong Du, and was killed by Liu Bei (先主). The *Wudi ji* records the same campaign but with the name written 蔡揚, and without saying he was killed: 「紹之未破也，使劉備略汝南，汝南賊共都等應之。遣蔡揚擊都，不利，為都所破」[40].

So the two accounts differ on one point: Liu Bei's biography says Cai Yang was killed by Liu Bei, while the *Wudi ji* says he attacked Gong Du (共都) and was defeated by Gong Du, without mentioning his death. They agree that this was a Runan operation against Liu Bei and Gong Du, not an encounter with Guan Yu.

由此看, in the *Sanguozhi*'s account Cai Yang's death belongs to Liu Bei's operations in Runan, and Guan Yu's return to Liu Bei (亡歸先主) is recorded separately, before Cai Yang's dispatch in Liu Bei's biography [2]; the records nowhere tie the two together. Since no relevant occurrence of 古城 appears in the text, the episode of Guan Yu killing Cai Yang at Gucheng cannot be grounded in the *Sanguozhi*: what the text gives is Liu Bei killing Cai Yang at Runan, and Guan Yu rejoining Liu Bei around the same period.

Guan Yu's own biography says that after Cao Cao captured him in 建安五年 (200) and he had killed Yan Liang at Baima to repay Cao Cao, he sealed up all the gifts, sent a letter of farewell, and went back to Liu Bei in Yuan Shao's army: 「羽盡封其所賜，拜書告辭，而奔先主於袁軍」[1]. It says nothing about killing Cai Yang, and nothing about a Gucheng.

Cai Yang's death is recorded in Liu Bei's biography, where Cao Cao sends him against Liu Bei and Gong Du in Runan: 「紹遣先主將本兵復至汝南，與賊龔都等合，眾數千人。曹公遣蔡陽擊之，為先主所殺」[2] — i.e. Cai Yang was killed by Liu Bei (先主), at Runan, not by Guan Yu at Gucheng. The *Wudi ji* (Annals of Emperor Wu) confirms the campaign, with the name written 蔡揚: 「紹之未破也，使劉備略汝南，汝南賊共都等應之。遣蔡揚擊都，不利，為都所破」[40].

So, per the records: Guan Yu did leave Cao Cao and rejoin Liu Bei in Yuan Shao's camp [1], and Cai Yang was sent by Cao Cao against Liu Bei/Gong Du in Runan and was killed by Liu Bei [2][40]. The two events are separate in the *Sanguozhi*; the "Gucheng" episode in which Guan Yu slays Cai Yang while escorting Liu Bei's wives back is a fictional embellishment. I found no occurrence of 古城 anywhere in the text.

Note also that the *Sanguozhi* does not say Guan Yu personally killed Cai Yang at all — that is the novel's invention. If you want, I can lay out the historical sequence of Guan Yu's 200 campaign (capture, Yan Liang, the return to Liu Bei) from the sources.

q: Who was Zhou Tai?
reply:
**Zhou Tai** is ambiguous in Chinese: the pinyin matches two different men in the *Sanguozhi* — 周泰 (Zhou Tai, style Youping), a Wu general, and 州泰 (Zhou Tai), a Wei general. Most readers asking the question mean the Wu one, but here is both.

**1. 周泰, style Youping (Wu)**

He was one of the "Twelve Tiger Ministers" of Wu (the collective biography is in Wu shu 10). He was from Xia Cai in Jiujiang commandery and first served Sun Ce alongside Jiang Qin: 「周泰字幼平，九江下蔡人也。與蔣欽隨孫策爲左右，服事恭敬，數戰有功。」[1] — "Zhou Tai, style Youping, a man of Xia Cai in Jiujiang. He and Jiang Qin attended Sun Ce as his close retainers, serving him respectfully, and won merit in many battles."

Sun Quan took a liking to him and asked to have him transferred to his own service. His most famous deed came when bandits caught Sun Quan nearly alone at Xuancheng: the bandits killed their way up to Sun Quan's side, and only Zhou Tai threw himself in front of him. 「惟泰奮激，投身衞權，膽氣倍人」[1], and 「是日無泰，權幾危殆」[1] — "Had there been no Zhou Tai that day, Sun Quan would have been in mortal danger." He took twelve wounds and was long in reviving. Sun Ce rewarded him with appointments as chief of Chungu and then Yichun.

Under Sun Quan he fought at Red Cliffs and at Nanjun against Cao Ren: 「後與周瑜、程普拒曹公於赤壁，攻曹仁於南郡。」[2] He also drove off Cao Cao at Ruxu and was left in command there as General Who Subdues the Caitiffs. When Zhu Ran and Xu Sheng, who were under him, refused to submit to his authority, Sun Quan personally came to Ruxu, made Zhou Tai strip and pointed out each scar, asking how it was got — after which they submitted [2]. The *Jiangbiao zhuan* adds Sun Quan's tearful words: 「幼平，卿爲孤兄弟戰如熊虎，不惜軀命，被創數十，膚如刻畫」[3] — "You fought for me and my brothers like a bear or a tiger, sparing neither body nor life; you have scores of wounds, your skin like carved lines." Sun Quan later made him Administrator of Hanzhong and General Who Spreads Might, Marquis of Lingyang; 「黃武中卒」[2] — he died in the Huangwu era. His son Zhou Shao and his younger brother Zhou Cheng carried on his troops and title [2]. Chen Shou's verdict on the group: 「凡此諸將，皆江表之虎臣，孫氏之所厚待也。」[5]

**2. 州泰 (Wei)**

A different man, from Nanyang, a contemporary of Deng Ai. He appears at the end of Deng Ai's biography: 「艾州里時輩南陽州泰，亦好立功業，善用兵，官至征虜將軍、假節都督江南諸軍事。景元二年薨，追贈衛將軍，諡曰壯侯。」[12] — "Zhou Tai of Nanyang, a man of Deng Ai's generation from the same province, likewise loved to establish merit, was skilled at using troops, and rose to General Who Subdues Caitiffs, Acting Credentials, supervising military affairs south of the Yangtze. He died in the second year of Jingyuan [261 CE] and was posthumously given the title General of the Guard, with the posthumous name Marquis Zhuang."

Pei Songzhi's note quoting the *Shiyu* gives his start: the Inspector of Jingzhou, Pei Qian, made him a 從事 and repeatedly sent him to Sima Yi (Sima Xuanwang) at Wan, by which he became known to Sima Yi; he guided the army in the campaign against Meng Da and was then summoned. After nine years of mourning for his father, mother and grandfather, Sima Yi held the post open for him and promoted him to Administrator of Xincheng after thirty-six days, which provoked Zhong Yao's jest and Zhou Tai's famous retort about "a monkey riding a clay ox" [11]. He later served as Inspector of Yan and Yu provinces, and in the Shouchun campaign of 257–258 he, as Inspector of Yanzhou, defeated Zhu Yi at Yangyuan and again broke him together with Shi Bao [19].

So: if the question is about a Wu "tiger minister" who shielded Sun Quan with his body, it is 周泰, style Youping. If it is about a Wei officer under Sima Yi who died in 261, it is 州泰.

review_raw:
拼音 Zhou Tai 在《三国志》里对应两个人：吴的周泰（字幼平）和魏的州泰。若问的是孙吴的虎臣，指的是周泰。

周泰字幼平，九江下蔡人，与蒋钦同为孙策的左右近侍：「周泰字幼平，九江下蔡人也。與蔣欽隨孫策爲左右，服事恭敬，數戰有功。」[1] 孙权喜爱他的为人，请求把他拨给自己使用（「權愛其爲人，請以自給」[1]）。他最有名的一件事是宣城救孙权：山贼数千人突然到来，刀锋已交到孙权身边，有的砍中马鞍，众人不能自定，只有周泰奋身护卫，「惟泰奮激，投身衞權，膽氣倍人」[1]；事后「身被十二創，良乆乃蘇」[1]，原文说「是日無泰，權幾危殆」[1]。孙策因此「補春穀長」，后来又补宜春长，「所在皆食其征賦」[1]。

在孙权手下，他随军讨黄祖有功，又与周瑜、程普在赤壁拒曹操、在南郡攻曹仁（「後與周瑜、程普拒曹公於赤壁，攻曹仁於南郡」[2]）。曹操出兵濡须，周泰赴击，曹操退兵，他留下督濡须，拜平虏将军[2]。当时朱然、徐盛等都在他部下而不服，孙权特地巡行到濡须坞，宴会上亲自行酒到周泰面前，命他解衣，亲手一一指着伤痕问起于何时，周泰回忆当年作战之处回答，第二天又「遣使者授以御蓋」，「於是盛等乃伏」[2]。裴注引《江表傳》记孙权握着他的手臂流泪，称他的字说：「幼平，卿爲孤兄弟戰如熊虎，不惜軀命，被創數十，膚如刻畫」[3]。后来孙权破关羽，欲图蜀，拜周泰汉中太守、奋威将军，封陵阳侯，「黃武中卒」[2]。传末记其子周邵以骑都尉领兵，黄龙二年卒，接着是「弟承領兵襲侯」[2]——由此看，接领兵与侯爵的是名"承"的人，原文只称"弟"，未点明是周泰之弟还是周邵之弟，这是推断。陈寿在本卷末评这批将领：「凡此諸將，皆江表之虎臣，孫氏之所厚待也。」[5]

另一位州泰是魏人，附见于邓艾传中：「艾州里時輩南陽州泰，亦好立功業，善用兵，官至征虜將軍、假節都督江南諸軍事。景元二年薨，追贈衛將軍，諡曰壯侯。」[12] 景元二年为公元 261 年。裴注引《世語》记他的起家：荆州刺史裴潜任他为从事，多次派他去见镇守宛城的司马宣王，由此被司马宣王所知；征孟达时他又为军队带路，于是被征召；他接连为父、母、祖父守丧九年，司马宣王留着职位等他，「至三十六日，擢為新城太守」；宴上尚书钟繇戏问他三十六天就拥麾盖守兵马之郡何其快，他答以「獼猴騎土牛，又何遲也」，后来历任兖、豫州刺史，「所在有籌算績效」[11]。诸葛诞据寿春叛、吴出兵救援时，他以魏兖州刺史的身份在阳渊阻击朱异，朱异败退被他追击，死伤二千人；后来又与监军石苞一起击破朱异[19]。

所以：问孙吴以身体护卫孙权的虎臣，是周泰（字幼平）；问司马懿麾下、景元二年去世的魏将，是州泰。

q: Tell me about Liu Yan.
reply:
"Liu Yan" matches three different men in the *Sanguozhi*: 刘焉, the warlord who became Governor of Yi Province; 刘琰, a Shu-Han general and official; and 刘延, who has no biography of his own. I take the first as the main subject.

**刘焉, styled Junlang**

A native of Jingling in Jiangxia, a descendant of the Han prince 鲁恭王, whose branch was enfeoffed at Jingling in the Yuanhe era of Emperor Zhang. In his youth he served in provincial and commandery offices, was made 中郎 as a member of the imperial clan, left office when his teacher 祝公 died, lived on Yangcheng Mountain where he 「積學教授」, was recommended as 賢良方正 and summoned to the 司徒府, and successively held 雒陽令, 冀州刺史, 南陽太守, 宗正 and 太常 [1].

Seeing Emperor Ling's misgovernment, he proposed: 「刺史、太守，貨賂為官，割剝百姓，以致離叛。可選清名重臣以為牧伯，鎮安方夏。」He privately sought the post of 交阯牧 to escape the coming troubles, but when the Palace Attendant 董扶 told him 「京師將亂，益州分野有天子氣」, 「焉聞扶言，意更在益州」[1].

When the Inspector of Yi, 郤儉, oppressed the people, his plan worked: he went out as 監軍使者, 領益州牧, 封陽城侯, with orders to arrest 郤儉 and punish him; 董扶 asked for the post of 蜀郡西部屬國都尉 and 趙韙 resigned as 太倉令, and both followed him [2]. A note quotes 《續漢書》 that at this time 劉虞 was given 幽州, 劉焉 益州, 劉表 荊州 and 賈琮 冀州, all 「海內清名之士」[4]; the same note quotes 《漢靈帝紀》 differently, that the Emperor 「敕焉為益州刺史」, that the former Inspectors 劉雋 and 郤儉 were both rapacious, that 「焉到便收攝行法」, and that 「焉受命而行，以道路不通，住荊州東界」[4].

In the revolt of 馬相 and 趙祗, who styled themselves Yellow Turbans and even called 馬相 Son of Heaven, the provincial official 賈龍 raised troops, broke them, and welcomed 劉焉; 劉焉 moved his seat to Mianzhu, where 「撫納離叛，務行寬惠，陰圖異計」. He sent 張魯 as 督義司馬 to hold Hanzhong, cut the mountain roads and kill the court's envoys, memorialized that 「米賊斷道，不得複通」, and used other pretexts to kill the strongmen 王咸, 李權 and more than ten others to establish his authority; the Administrator of Jianwei, 任岐, and 賈龍 then turned against him and he killed both [8]. A note from 《英雄記》 says he raised troops but did not join the campaign against Dong Zhuo, 「保州自守」, and that when Dong Zhuo sent 趙謙 against the province and 趙謙 persuaded 賈龍 to turn back and attack him, 劉焉 sent out the 青羌 to fight and so was able to defeat and kill them [7].

His ambitions grew: he 「造作乘輿車具千馀乘」, and 劉表 memorialized that this resembled Zixia at Xihe, whose bearing made men suspect a sage. His sons 劉範, 劉誕 and 劉璋 were at Chang'an with Emperor Xian, only 劉瑁 staying with him; the Emperor sent 劉璋 to reason with him and he kept 劉璋 from returning. When 馬騰 rose at Mei, 劉焉 and 劉範 conspired with him to attack Chang'an; the plot leaked, 劉範 fled to Huaili and was killed, 馬騰 withdrew to Liang, 劉誕 was arrested and executed, and 龐羲 gathered 劉焉's grandsons and brought them into Shu [21].

A fire from heaven burned his city and all his equipages; he moved his seat to Chengdu, and grieving for his sons and shaken by the portent, 「興平元年，癰疽發背而卒」. The great official 趙韙 and others then put forward his son 劉璋 as Inspector of Yi [6].

reply:
"Zhang Yi" is ambiguous in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*: the pinyin matches three different Shu-Han men. Here is what each is known for.

**1. Zhang Yi 张裔, courtesy name Junsi 君嗣** (Shu, ch. 11)
He was a Chengdu man, learned in the *Gongyang Commentary* and the *Shi ji*/*Han shu*. Under Liu Zhang he was sent as envoy to Liu Bei; later he served as Administrator of Ba and then of Yizhou, but the southern leader Yong Kai seized him and handed him over to Wu, where he remained in hiding for years. Zhuge Liang had Deng Zhi request his return, and the exchange with Sun Quan on his release is his famous episode: when Sun Quan mocked Shu customs, Zhang Yi answered that "the widowed daughter of the Zhuo family was still better than Zhu Maichen's wife," then, regretting he had not played the fool, hurried away by double marches before Sun Quan's pursuers could catch him「裔出閣，深悔不能陽愚，即便就船，倍道兼行」[3]. Back in Shu he became Marshal of the Retinue and, with Zhuge Liang in Hanzhong, Keeper of the Rear Office (留府長史) [2]. He died in the 8th year of Jianxing (230). Chen Shou praised him as "intelligent, both resourceful and kind" (贊張君嗣) [14].

**2. Zhang Yi 张嶷, courtesy name Boqi 伯岐** (Shu, ch. 13)
The most famous of the three. A man of Nanchongguo in Ba commandery, he first made his name as a youth by carrying the magistrate's wife through bandits at the risk of his life [11]. He is best known for a long, successful tenure as Administrator of Yuexi/Yuejun in the south — the *Yibu Qijiu zhuan* says he was there fifteen years and the region was "peaceful and serene," so that when he was recalled the Yi people clung to his carriage and wept「夷民戀慕，扶轂泣涕」[16], and after his death they built temples to him [16]. He also put down the rebellion of Liu Zhou and, per the *Yibu Qijiu zhuan*, engineered the surrender of the Wenshan Qiang by trickery [17]. He died fighting in 254 (17th year of Yanxi), in Jiang Wei's campaign against Xu Zhi at Didao「嶷臨陣隕身，然其所殺傷亦過倍」[16].

**3. Zhang Yi 张翼, courtesy name Bogong 伯恭** (Shu, ch. 15)
A Wuyang man of Qianwei, great-grandson of the Excellency Zhang Hao. He is known above all as the general who *opposed* Jiang Wei's repeated campaigns. As commander of the Xiangjiang troops against Liu Zhou he refused to abandon his post before his replacement arrived, saying public business must not be neglected because of his own dismissal「豈可以黜退之故而廢公家之務乎」[10]. In 255 he argued at court that Shu was too small and its people too weary for more war, and after Jiang Wei's great victory over Wang Jing at Didao he urged him to stop, warning that going further would ruin the achievement — Jiang Wei angrily accused him of "drawing legs on a snake"「為蛇畫足」[21]. Chen Shou's verdict: he "withstood Jiang Wei's keen edge"「張翼亢姜維之銳」[23]. He surrendered with Jiang Wei to Zhong Hui at Fu in 263 and was killed by mutinous troops in Chengdu the following year [21].

So the answer depends on which Zhang Yi you mean — if you had a particular one in mind (southern campaigns, rear-office administration, or opposition to Jiang Wei), tell me and I can go deeper.

「张仪」这个拼音在《三国志》里对应三位蜀汉人物，各自的知名之处如下。

**张裔，字君嗣，蜀郡成都人**[1]。他「治《公羊春秋》，博涉《史》、《漢》」[1]。刘璋时举孝廉，任鱼复长，后「為璋奉使詣先主」[1]；先主「以裔巴郡太守」，后「乃以裔為益州太守」，雍闿不肯臣服，把张裔捆了送给孙权，「於是遂送裔於權」[1]。他在吴国多年，「裔自至吳數年，流徒伏匿，權未之知也」[3]。诸葛亮「遣鄧芝使吳，亮令芝言次可從權請裔」[3]。临行时孙权拿卓氏寡女私奔司马相如的事讥讽蜀地风俗，张裔答「愚以為卓氏之寡女，猶賢於買臣之妻」[3]；出来后后悔没能装傻，「裔出閣，深悔不能陽愚，即便就船，倍道兼行」，孙权果然派人追赶，「裔已入永安界數十里，追者不能及」[3]。回蜀后「丞相亮以為參軍，署府事，又領益州治中從事」；诸葛亮出驻汉中，「裔以射聲校尉領留府長史」[2]，「加輔漢將軍，領長史如故」，建兴八年去世（230 年）[2]。杨戏的《季汉辅臣赞》里有「贊張君嗣」一首[14]。

**张嶷，字伯岐，巴郡南充国人**[11]。他二十岁做县功曹时，山寇攻县，县长弃家逃亡，「嶷冒白刃，攜負夫人，夫人得免」，因此显名[11]。建兴五年，绵竹山贼张慕等劫掠军资，他「度其鳥散，難以戰禽。乃詐與和親，剋期置酒」，趁酒酣亲率左右斩张慕等五十余级，十天内清平[11]。他「拜為牙門將，屬馬忠，北討汶山叛羌，南平四郡蠻夷」[11]；裴注引《益部耆旧传》记他讨汶山羌时攻不下石门的险隘，便「使譯告曉之」，羌人首领出降、供给粮秣；后来南夷刘胄反叛，他随马忠讨伐，「戰鬥常冠軍首，遂斬冑」[17]。他长期治理南方一郡，「在郡十五年，邦域安穆」，被征召赴成都时「夷民戀慕，扶轂泣涕」[16]。延熙十七年（254 年），他随姜维出陇西，与魏将徐质交锋，「嶷臨陣隕身」[16]。他死后「南土越巂民夷聞嶷死，無不悲泣，為嶷立廟，四時水旱輒祀之」[16]。

**张翼，字伯恭，犍为武阳人**，「高祖父司空浩，曾祖父廣陵太守綱」[10]。建兴九年任庲降都督，刘胄叛乱，他举兵讨伐，正逢被征召当还，部下都劝他赶紧回去请罪，他说「豈可以黜退之故而廢公家之務乎」，照旧统领不懈，接替的人到了才动身，马忠靠他打下的基础消灭了刘胄[10]。他后来官至征西大将军，延熙元年入为尚书，进封都亭侯[10]。延熙十八年与姜维一同回成都，「維議復出軍，唯翼廷爭，以為國小民勞，不宜黷武」[21]。姜维到狄道大破魏雍州刺史王经，张翼劝「可止矣，不宜復進，進或毀此大功」，姜维大怒，说他「為蛇畫足」[21]。景耀二年迁左车骑将军，领冀州刺史；景耀六年（263 年）与姜维同在剑阁，一起到涪县向钟会投降，「明年正月，隨會至成都，為亂兵所殺」[21]。陈寿评他「張翼亢姜維之銳」[23]。

所以看你要问的是哪一位：以南方平叛和治理边郡知名的是张嶷，以留府长史和出使应对知名的是张裔，以反对姜维连年用兵知名的是张翼。
